extracted.intended_audience: researchers in bibliometrics/informetrics, scientometrics, information science, and NLP researchers building citation classifiers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, conducting, or evaluating citation analyses that go beyond raw citation counts by using citation contexts, functions, polarity, location, linguistic features, and automated classifiers to measure citation influence and meaning. Applies to empirical studies and development of citation-function/polarity classifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use citation content/context analyses (not just counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the citation context to provide additional information about how a cited paper has been used in the citing paper; citation content/context analyses are proposed as complementary methods to traditional quantitative citation analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: conventional citation analysis treats citations equally and overlooks varied reasons/functions of citations. Operationalizations include the position of the citation, the semantics surrounding the reference, and the words around citations. Use content/context analyses to describe relationships between citing and cited works and to evaluate impact qualitatively and quantitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify citation functions and citation polarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the function(s) of each citation (e.g. use, criticize, extend, compare, background, substantiation) and its polarity (negative, neutral, positive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many studies develop classification schemes and automated classifiers for functions and polarity. Automated recognition of citation functions has potential to improve indices and IR. Report scheme definitions and classifier performance; consider that citations can have multiple functions and mixed polarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish influential (important) vs non-influential citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether a citation had substantial influence on the citing work (important/influential) versus being perfunctory or incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results show only a small percentage of citations are influential (examples: Valenzuela et al. 14.6%; Zhu et al. 10.3%). Predictive features include number of times a paper is cited within the citing paper. Studies should operationalize 'influential' clearly and report prevalence in sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze citation location within the citing document (IMRaD/section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the location of a citation in the citing article (e.g. Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) as a feature for understanding citation function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMRaD structure is an important feature for classifiers; some functions/polarities concentrate in particular sections (e.g. methodology citations higher in Methods). Include section-level metadata (when available) in models and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the number of times a reference appears in the citing paper (recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use how often a cited work is mentioned within a single citing document as an indicator—recurrence often correlates with influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple citation instances within the same paper are a strong indicator of influence (e.g. Pride & Knoth). Extract and count all citances per citing paper rather than relying on a single citation instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate citation-context window size
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how many sentences around the citation to include (one sentence, +/- one, three sentences, four sentences, etc.) when extracting context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer contexts (three sentences, four sentences) often improve performance for IR and classification tasks versus single-sentence contexts. Cite and justify context-window choice; empirical comparisons (Ritchie et al., Yousif et al.) favor larger windows for some tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use machine-readable full text (XML) and automated data processing for large-scale studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer XML/formatted full-text sources and automated pipelines to extract citation instances and associated metadata for large datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-readable formats (XML) provide exact citation locations and structured metadata, enabling large-scale citation-context analyses and classifier training. Use sources like PubMed Central, PLOS, ACL Anthology, Microsoft Academic, Elsevier ConSyn, etc., and document data provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report data source, sample size, and data-processing method
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly document databases used (WoS, Scopus, PubMed, ACL, publisher XML), sample sizes, and whether processing was automated or manual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's methods section should describe search strategies, deduplication, screening decisions, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. This transparency supports reproducibility and assessment of bias (e.g. database coverage, discipline skew).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and mitigate subjectivity in manual annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When using manual coding for citation functions/contexts, recognize annotator subjectivity and measure inter-annotator agreement; address disagreements appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual analyses can produce contradictory results due to subjective judgments and annotators not expert in the domain. Report inter-annotator agreement, consider removing ambiguous instances to improve classifier performance, and provide annotation guidelines/examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine quantitative and qualitative features for richer measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate quantitative citation counts with qualitative context/content features to better capture a paper's impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation content analysis takes into account both quantitative and qualitative factors (how one cites). Use mixed-method approaches where appropriate and justify how combined metrics improve validity over counts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include linguistic and semantic features (verbs, hedges, lexical patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze words, verbs, hedging cues, and semantic roles in citation contexts to characterize citation intent and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies find hedging words more frequent in citation contexts; verb distribution varies by section. Feature engineering should include lexical n-grams, hedges, semantic role labels, and rhetorical markers to improve classification of function/polarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for disciplinary and language differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for differences in citation behavior across disciplines (natural sciences vs social sciences/humanities) and possibly across languages or national practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation functions, polarity distributions, and prevalence of perfunctory vs confirmative citations vary by discipline; models and interpretations should be stratified or adjusted accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model document, author, and journal-level features influencing citing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include metadata on cited/citing documents, author characteristics, and journal features as predictors or controls in citation studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tahamtan & Bornmann's synoptic model highlights document features, author features, journal features, decision rules, and reasons. Examples: outlet policy, co-authorship, outlet type, favored paradigms all influence citation patterns and should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for multiple citations within a sentence and complex sentence structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle cases where sentences contain several citations or where parts of a sentence refer to different works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design extraction and labeling protocols that segment citances appropriately; consider dependency parsing or manual adjudication for multi-citation sentences to avoid misattribution of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use validated classifiers and report performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing automated classifiers for citation function/polarity/influence, validate models and report metrics like accuracy, precision, recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide training/test splits, cross-validation, and performance numbers (e.g. Teufel et al. reported ~75% for functions, 83% for polarity; Small's discovery classifier reached 94% accuracy). Discuss limitations and error analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using simple keyword heuristics (e.g. discovery words) without validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume presence of specific words guarantees a conceptual label (e.g. 'discovery' words imply discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small et al. found only 46% of citances with discovery words were true discoveries; keyword-based classifiers can be high-accuracy when validated but must be evaluated against gold annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design transparent search and screening strategies for literature-based studies
rubrics_metrics.description: For literature reviews or meta-analyses of citation studies, specify search strings, databases searched, deduplication steps, and screening criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewed study used title-limited searches with explicit search terms and documented deduplication and screening (188 retrieved → 41 included). Such transparency reduces selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social and behavioral motives in models (trust, knowing authors, editorial policies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate citer motivation variables—social relations, trust, knowing cited authors, publisher/editor policies—when explaining citation behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey/interview studies show citing reasons include relevance, importance, knowing authors, publisher policy, and editor decisions. Where possible, collect or proxy these variables to enrich explanatory models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize citation context and keyword co-occurrence to interpret citation landscapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use network/keyword co-occurrence and visualization techniques to map contexts in which authors cite a given body of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Bornmann et al.) show contextual keyword networks help interpret how a scholar's work is cited across topics. Visualizations should be accompanied by methodological notes on node/edge construction and thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating all citations as equal in evaluative bibliometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that citation counts alone are insufficient and that evaluative bibliometrics should incorporate citation-context insights for more meaningful results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because citations arise from varied scientific and non-scientific reasons, bibliometric indicators should be adjusted or complemented by context-aware measures to better reflect influence and quality.
